question: Why does a transformer need positional encodings while an RNN does not?
options: Attention treats its input as a set (permutation equivariant), while an RNN reads tokens in order
RNNs use embeddings and transformers do not
explanation: Self-attention weights depend only on content. Without positions, shuffling the input just shuffles the output.

question: How is a learned absolute position embedding used?
options: It is multiplied with the attention weights
A trainable vector for each position is added to the token embedding at the input
It is applied only to the values
explanation: x_i = embed(token_i) + p_i, with p a trainable n_max x d matrix.

question: Without any positional information, the reversal model reached about 27% token accuracy. What strategy gives that number?
options: Predicting the most frequent token of the sequence at every position
explanation: It can only compute functions of the bag of tokens. Guessing the mode is correct for about a quarter of positions with 12 tokens over 10 symbols; random guessing would give 10%.

question: Which property of the sinusoidal encoding did the script verify?
options: Its values grow linearly with position
PE(p + k) is a fixed rotation of PE(p), and PE(p) . PE(p + k) depends only on k
explanation: Each dimension pair is a sine/cosine at one frequency, so a shift rotates each pair by a fixed angle.

question: Where is RoPE applied?
options: Added to the token embeddings once at the input
To the queries and keys inside every attention layer, as a position-dependent rotation
explanation: Rotating q at position m and k at position n makes their dot product depend on n - m.

question: RoPE only encodes relative offsets, yet it solved reversal, which needs absolute positions. How?
options: The edges reveal absolute position: position 0 only sees keys at positive offsets and position 11 only at negative ones
explanation: With bidirectional attention, the set of available offsets differs by position, so absolute position can be inferred.
